opener.heading: Week 12: Baby Animals & New Beginnings 🐣
about: This week runs on new arrivals: lambs on wobbly legs, ducklings, tadpoles, a bean splitting open in a jam jar, and Kreston, who at nine months is doing what Azlyn did three years ago. She spends most of it looking after something smaller than she is. Eight toy animals get breakfast, a nursery goes up in the corner of a room, six nests go up on the counter, and her brother gets his banana mashed by hand.

Saturday is the spring equinox. Day and night run the same length, and from Sunday the light wins, which is worth telling her while you are out under the bare trees looking for last year's nests. Nothing else this week needs a date on it, and the rest of it runs on odd socks, dried beans and masking tape.
azlyn: Baby animals and their grown-ups. Lamb and sheep, duckling and duck, and the two pairs she cannot guess yet.
One thing for each. A bowl per animal, a lid per mouth, a toy per nest, counted and then counted back.
Balance and control across cushions, along a low wall, over a rolled towel and off the floor without her hands.
Giving an instruction somebody follows. She says it, you do that exact thing, and she hears where her own words went wrong.
What a seed does out of sight. She splits a bean open, plants seven more against the glass and marks a box on the chart every afternoon.
you: The vestibular system, and why she spins until she falls over
Children understand fairness before they understand generosity
Directing others is how a child rehearses being in charge of herself
Choosing three from seven is real cognitive work
A daily ritual of checking teaches more than the plant does
Let her hold a wrong theory for a while
shopping: Plain paper, a stack of about 25 sheets
2 pens, for writing her words down
A clipboard, or card and a bulldog clip
3 odd socks you do not want back, plus a plain fourth one for Kreston
4 sofa cushions, 1 blanket and 1 rolled bath towel
Every toy animal in the house, and a doll
8 bottle lids, egg cups or small pots
A teaspoon, a tablespoon, a table knife and a fork
A baby spoon, and an old bottle or sippy cup for the doll
Plates, forks and cups for laying the table
Newspaper, 2 sheets to tear into strips
A scrap of fabric you can tear up
A mesh produce bag, the net kind lemons come in
Paper cups or empty yogurt cups, 6
3 clean jam jars, one with a lid that screws on tight
Dried lima beans, 1 bag (white beans only, never raw red kidney)
Dried lentils, a handful, for the Nowruz saucer
A high shelf or a cupboard top she cannot reach, cleared on Wednesday
Baby photos of Azlyn, on your phone or printed out
One outfit Azlyn wore as a baby, if you still have one
Dried grass, moss and thin twigs (gather these on the walks)
A few feathers if you come across any
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 9 months this week. He pulls himself up on anything at hip height, picks up a single raisin between finger and thumb, and waves at people, who wave back. The pincer grip arrived this month, which is why the beans, the oats and the small toys stay above his reach all week.

days.title: Wobbly Legs
days.prepTonight: Stack four sofa cushions by the sofa, leave the masking tape and a marker on the table, and dig out three odd socks you do not want back. They become animals tomorrow.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Story of the Night She Was Born

opening.title: Five Stations on the Floor
opening.need: 1 roll masking tape · 5 sheets of paper · 1 marker.
steps: Write one animal across each sheet in big letters: LAMB, DUCKLING, TADPOLE, FOAL, PUPPY. She holds the paper flat.
Walk the room together and let her choose where each sign lands. Tape all five to the floor in a loop with a clear run between them.
Ask her how a lamb walks on its first morning. Copy whatever she shows you, then tell her the course opens at 9:15.

main.title: The Newborn Legs Course
materials: 5 sheets of paper and a marker for the station signs
steps: Lamb. Lay the four cushions end to end under the sign. She crosses them upright, no hands down. A lamb stands inside an hour of being born and wobbles all day.
Duckling. Set the two chairs a stride apart and tape a lane between them. Feet wide, hands flat at her sides, tiny steps. Go through it first and let her tell you what you got wrong.
Tadpole. She lies on her tummy under the sign with the blanket spread ahead of her and gets across it with no hands and no knees down. Belly and legs only.
Foal. She lies flat on her back and stands up without putting a hand on the floor. Go first, and let her watch an adult fail at it twice.
Puppy. Roll the bath towel and lay it down. She rolls over it, gets up, spins three times and stops.
Run the whole loop three times in order. Call out the station names as she reaches them and let her invent a sixth animal on the last lap.
main.tip: Run the course yourself at least once. Your knees give out at the foal station.

outside.title: Walking the Low Wall
paras: Find the lowest wall, curb or log on your route and let her walk the length of it with one hand in yours. March gives you a dry top most mornings and a puddle at the bottom. Go the whole way, turn round, and come back holding the other hand. Look under the hedge for the green coming through last year's brown.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulling himself up on anything that will hold him. Park him at the sofa arm beside the lamb station so he can haul himself upright and drop back down while Azlyn wobbles across the cushions. Out on the walk he waves at people from the stroller now.

second.title: When Azlyn Was New
second.intro: Kreston is doing this week what Azlyn did three years ago. She has never seen the evidence.
materials: Phone or printed photos of Azlyn as a baby
1 outfit she wore as a baby, if you still have one
A pen, and a strip of masking tape for the doorframe
steps: Sit on the floor with Kreston between you and go through the baby photos of Azlyn. Say her name every time. She will need telling twice that the baby is her.
Lay the old outfit flat beside Kreston. Let her hold it against him, then against herself.
Measure her with the tape, then measure him. Say both numbers out loud and write them on the first sheet.
Draw round her bare foot on the second sheet. Draw round his beside it while he is on your lap.
Ask her what she thinks she could do when she was Kreston's size, and what Kreston will do when he is her size. Let the wrong answers stand.

Stick the strip of tape to the doorframe. Mark the top of her head on it, lay Kreston flat against the frame and mark his length under hers, date both, and pin the sheet of feet up beside them at her height.
second.tip: A baby who is her and also not her is a hard idea at three. Close the phone if the photos upset her and stay on the feet and the tape measure.

alternatives: Baby photos on the sofa and nothing else.
Hand and foot outlines for the whole house on one sheet.
Sort her old clothes into a keep pile and a pass-on pile with her.
outAgain: The café, cake and a window seat, and count how many babies come through the door
The park, for the swings and the mud under the slide
A friend's house, if anyone else is having a long one
The same low wall again in the late light, this time with no hand

aroundWorld.title: Spring New Years 🌱
paras: Half the world starts its year in spring. Nowruz falls on Sunday across Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia, and families lay a table with seven symbolic things on it, one of them a dish of wheat sprouted at home. Thailand welcomes Songkran in April with a country-wide water fight. In southern India, Ugadi opens the year with a paste carrying six tastes at once.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Wet a handful of lentils, spread them on a saucer lined with damp paper towels, and let Azlyn keep them damp. Green shoots in four days.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Nowruz means "new day," and the year turns with the spring equinox.

days.krestonPM: Hand him the tape measure once you have finished with it. His pincer grip arrived this month and a stiff tape with a hook on the end beats most toys. In the café, sit him facing the counter. He waves at 9 months, somebody always waves back, and he finds that enormous.

insight.headline: The vestibular system, and why she spins until she falls over.
paras: Azlyn has an organ in each inner ear reading every tilt, drop and turn her head makes, and it feeds the same system that will let her sit still in a chair at five. Spinning, rolling and hanging upside down flood it with input, and she seeks that input out because the system is still calibrating. A morning of rolling over a towel and staggering across cushions does more for her balance than an hour of being told to be careful. She will not always stop on her own. Dizziness reads as fun before it reads as too much, so keep the bursts short and end it before she does.

days.safety: Spinning leaves her staggering with no idea where the furniture is, so clear the coffee table and any hard corner out of the puppy station first and keep it to three turns. Kreston pulls to stand on anything at 9 months, including a dining chair with nothing holding it down. Weight the course chairs or keep him the other side of the room.

days.title: The Noise Every Baby Makes
days.prepTonight: Put the three socks, both markers and a paper bag on the table, and check you have oats, raisins and a ripe banana in for tomorrow.

schedule.name: The First Bee of the Year

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Sock Babies in a Box

opening.title: Which Animal Says That
opening.need: the table you are already sitting at · your voice · hers.
steps: Make a noise with your eyes shut and let her name the animal. Start with the easy ones, then do a bad one on purpose and let her tell you it was wrong.
Swap. She makes the noise, you guess, and you get one wrong.
Ask which noises a baby makes and which the mother makes. Do both, high and low, and tell her three of them move in at 9:15.

main.title: Three Socks, Three Babies
materials: 3 odd socks you do not want back
1 paper bag to keep them in
steps: Put a sock on your hand, thumb under and fingers over, and open the mouth once. Hand it to her. She has the grip inside four seconds.
She decides which sock is the lamb, which the duckling, which the puppy. Write the name on the sole of each one so nobody argues at four o'clock.
Lay each sock flat with a folded sheet of paper inside so the marker cannot come through onto the table. She draws the eyes, and you do what she asks for after that and nothing she does not.
Fold strips of masking tape into ears for the lamb and the puppy and a beak for the duckling, and tape them on while the sock is still flat.
Now the voices. She invents one for each and has to keep it. Ask the lamb a question and answer as the lamb, then hand it back and let her take over.
Introduce them to each other, then walk all three over to Kreston and let them talk to him. He answers in his own noise, which is the whole joke.
main.tip: Commit to the voices and hold your own. She will drop hers a dozen times and come back to it.

outside.title: The First Bee of the Year
paras: Today the day and the night run the same length, and from tomorrow the light wins. The first bees come out on a morning like this, so take her to the crocuses in the grass and wait. A queen bumblebee is fat and slow this early and works one flower at a time. Count how many she visits before she goes, both of you a step back.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and babbling in long strings that rise and fall like sentences. Give him a fourth sock, one with no face on it, and let him chew it while the three animals talk over his head. Answer his noises as though they were words. He waves now, so have each sock wave at him and give him a second to wave one back.

second.title: The Lost Baby Game
second.intro: The three animals get lost round the house and she is the only one who can call them home.
materials: 1 laundry basket as the home nest
1 dish towel for covering hiding places
A blanket for the last hiding place
steps: Put the laundry basket in the middle of the floor. That is the nest, and every found baby goes in it.
She sits in the nest with her hands over her eyes while you hide all three. One in plain sight, one behind something, one under the dish towel.
She is the mother now. She has to call each one in its own noise, and you answer from the hiding place in that animal's voice, no louder than a whisper.
Let her hunt. Answer every time she calls and stay quiet when she does not.
Swap over. She hides them, you call, and you use the wrong voice at least once so she can correct you.
Last round, hide yourself under the blanket with all three and let her find the lot at once.
Count them into the paper bag together. Three out, three back.
second.tip: Whisper the answering voice. She has to hold still to place a sound, and it buys you ten minutes of a three-year-old standing quiet in a hallway with her head on one side.

alternatives: Hide the socks in one room only and stop after two rounds.
Hide her shoes instead and let her call for those.
Put on a show behind the sofa back with all three.
outAgain: A bus ride to nowhere in particular, front seat by the window, back on the next one
The park, and take one sock animal in your pocket for the swing
The duck pond, to look for this year's first ducklings on the water
The pet store window, for the rabbits and the noise of the birds
days.krestonPM: Take him on the bus in the carrier facing out. At 9 months an engine underneath him and a window full of moving houses is plenty, and twenty minutes each way is the whole trip. Back home, sit him in the empty laundry basket with the fourth sock while Azlyn plays round him.

insight.headline: Silliness is real social work.
paras: Azlyn spends this morning giving voices to three socks, and the daft parts carry the load. Holding a character means she keeps two things in her head at once, what the sock is doing and what she is doing, and that split is the foundation of understanding another mind. Playing the mother animal calling for a lost baby puts her inside somebody else's feeling, ten minutes at a time. She also watches your face to check that a joke has landed, which is how she learns to read a room. An adult who commits to the silly voice teaches more than an adult who supervises it.

days.safety: Marker caps go back on between socks and the pen stays out of reach. Check each sock for peeled tape before it goes near Kreston, and all three stay with you during the hiding game. Bees get watched, never touched.

days.title: Feeding Time
days.prepTonight: Set the tray, the oats, the raisins and eight bottle lids on the counter, pile every toy animal in the house beside them, and put four to six shoeboxes aside for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Frog Eggs at the Pond Edge

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Water Cups

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Washing the Doll in the Bath

opening.title: Counting Out the Mouths
opening.need: every toy animal in the house · 1 tray · 8 bottle lids or egg cups.
steps: Bring the animals to the table and let her line them along the edge of the tray, facing in.
Count the mouths with her finger landing on each one. Count again in a different order and let her find that the number holds.
Give her the lids and ask for one in front of each animal. Let her run out or have spares over, and leave it that way until 9:15.

main.title: Breakfast for Eight Animals
materials: 8 bottle lids, egg cups or small pots as bowls
steps: Set the row of animals and their bowls on the tray. Tip the oats into one big bowl in the middle and give her the tablespoon.
One spoonful each, along the row, until the oats run out. Say nothing about the amounts. She works left to right and the last two go short.
Ask what to do about the animal at the end and do whatever she says. She may raid the full bowls, top up the empty one, or rule that the last animal is not hungry.
Raisins next, and there are not enough for one each. Hand her the handful and stand back. Ask her the reason once the last one is down, and let the answer stand.
Water with the teaspoon, one spoon per bowl.
Feed them. Every animal gets held to its bowl and makes its noise, then the lot goes back into one bowl for 4:15.
main.tip: Resist evening up the bowls behind her. The uneven row is the activity.

outside.title: Frog Eggs at the Pond Edge
paras: Frogs lay in the last cold weeks of March. Go to the pond, a ditch or any still water and look in the shallows for clumps of jelly with a black dot in every blob. Count the dots in one clump until you both give up. An empty pond gives you water striders and green weed instead. Come back in three weeks for the tadpoles, and every walk in between to see whether the dots have moved.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and picks up single small things between finger and thumb, which is why the oats stay on the table and he stays in the high chair. Give him his own bowl upside down and a metal teaspoon to bang on it. At the water's edge he stays in the stroller.

second.title: Mashing Banana for Kreston
second.intro: She has fed eight animals who eat nothing. This afternoon she makes the real food for Kreston.
steps: Wash both your hands where she can see it happening. Kreston goes in the high chair upright, bib on.
She peels the banana. Start the top for her and let the rest be her problem.
Half the banana into a bowl for her to mash with the fork. Let her carry on past the point where it is smooth.
Pinch the other half into pea-sized pieces and lay them on his tray. He picks those up himself, one at a time, with his new grip.
She loads the baby spoon and offers it. He turns his head or opens his mouth, and she has no say in which. Sit beside her while she works out that he decides.
The doll gets the second bowl and the old bottle. That baby holds still and takes everything.
Damp washcloth at the end. Hands first, then face, and he will object to the face.
second.tip: He will wear a good deal of it and she will mind more than he does. Say before you start that the mess is how a baby learns to eat.

alternatives: Mash for the doll only and let Kreston have his food as usual.
Let her set out his finger pieces and skip the spoon.
Sort the raisins and oats into pots on a tray, no animals.
outAgain: A sunset walk, which the clocks going forward have pushed to after dinner
Back to the pond to check the eggs are where you left them
The field path, to look for lambs in the far corner
Scooter round the block while the light lasts
days.krestonPM: His pincer grip is three weeks old. Give him ten minutes with the banana pieces before anybody offers a spoon, and let him drop most of them, because at 9 months the dropping is research. On the walk, face him forward so he can watch Azlyn run ahead and come back.

insight.headline: Children understand fairness before they understand generosity.
paras: Azlyn will notice the short bowl at the end of the row before you say a word, and she will mind. Three-year-olds keep a close count of equal shares and object to a split that goes against them, which is why the last animal on the tray is the one she argues about. Giving away her own portion so somebody else has enough is a separate skill, and it lands closer to five or six. Handing her the raisins and letting her sort out an impossible division does more than an instruction to share, because she has to hold the problem herself. Her solutions will look odd. They are the working, and the working is what matters.

days.safety: Kreston is 9 months and eats with a pincer grip, so his pieces stay soft and no bigger than a pea, he sits upright the whole time, and Azlyn hands him food only while you are watching her do it. Raisins and dry oats go up on a high shelf between the morning tray and the 4:15 scooping, and at 4:15 they stay on the table with Kreston in the high chair beside her. At the pond, hold her hand at the edge and keep Kreston in the stroller.

days.title: Azlyn Is In Charge
days.prepTonight: Stack the shoeboxes and the laundry basket in a clear corner, put fresh batteries in the flashlight, and save the net bag the lemons came in for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: You Do Exactly What She Says

opening.title: The Badge and the Clipboard
opening.need: 1 sheet of card · 1 marker · masking tape · a clipboard, or card with a bulldog clip.
steps: Cut a badge out of the card. She says what it should say and you write it, spelling out the letters as you go.
Tape it to her sweater. It stays on all morning and she will check it is still there about nine times.
Load the clipboard with three sheets of paper and hand it over. Tell her the nursery opens at 9:15 and she is the one running it.

main.title: The Nursery She Runs
materials: Dish towels and washcloths for bedding
1 marker and paper for name cards
steps: She picks the corner. Tape the outline of the nursery on the floor along the walls she chooses and put the laundry basket inside it.
Shoeboxes become beds. She decides which animal sleeps in which and how the dish towels and washcloths go in.
Write a name card for every animal as she dictates the names. She tapes them on herself, upside down in places.
One of them is sick this morning. Ask her which. Give her the flashlight for the check-up and let her name the illness and the cure.
Take her through what each one eats and when, writing the list on the clipboard as she talks. Read it back and let her correct you.
Ask for a job. Do the job she gives you, at the speed she sets, and check with her before you finish.
main.tip: Every time she asks you something, hand it back: you're in charge, what should we do?

outside.title: A Fence for the Lamb
paras: March ground is soft enough to push sticks into, so find a patch of bare earth or a border and build a pen. Sticks pushed in a circle, gaps small enough that nothing gets out, a gate she can lift. Put a stone inside as the lamb. On the way home count the gaps in a real fence and see what holds its gate shut.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and cruising along the edge of anything solid. Set one shoebox at the very edge of the nursery as his, loaded with a washcloth and a soft toy she has signed off. He empties it and you fill it back up.

second.title: You Do Exactly What She Says
second.intro: Three real jobs, and she gives every instruction. You carry out what she says and nothing she has not said.
materials: Paper and a pen to write her instructions down word for word
Plates, forks and cups for the table
steps: Set the rule out loud once: you do what she says, in the order she says it, and nothing else. Then stop explaining and wait.
Job one, a jam sandwich. Write each instruction down as she gives it. Follow it to the letter, so put the jam on the bread means jam on the bag the bread is in.
Let that sit. Do not rescue it. She fixes it with a new instruction.
Job two, laying the table. She counts the people and calls out how many of everything, and you fetch what she asks for and no more.
Job three, Kreston's bottle or cup. Tell her which parts you have to do yourself and why, then do the rest on her word.
Read the whole sheet back to her at the end, in order, including the instruction about the bag.
She signs it. A scribble counts. Pin it up in the kitchen for Joseph to read.
second.tip: Follow the wrong instruction with a straight face. Jam on a bread bag is where she works out that her own words caused it.

alternatives: One job only, the sandwich, and stop there.
She directs you round an obstacle course while you keep your eyes shut.
Let her tell you what to draw, line by line.
outAgain: The green space with a ball, and she picks the game and the rules
The park, and she chooses which way round and what you do first
A walk past the pen you built this morning to see whether it held
The playground with the big slide, for the running she has not done today
days.krestonPM: He gets his bottle from the run she directed. Tell her that. At 9 months he holds it himself for a stretch before it wanders. Out on the grass, sit him down and roll the ball to him from a meter away. He will not roll it back, but he bats it, watches where it goes and waves at it.

insight.headline: Directing others is how a child rehearses being in charge of herself.
paras: Azlyn spends most of her day being told when to eat, when to leave and what to put on. Twenty minutes of running a nursery flips that, and the flip does real work. Giving an order out loud means holding a plan in mind, putting it in order and saying it in words somebody else can follow, which is the same machinery she will use on herself when she has to wait or stop or start something hard. Bossiness at three is a skill arriving. Give it an hour a week with a clipboard and it has somewhere to go.

days.safety: Kreston is on the floor inside the nursery with a month-old pincer grip, and the small toy animals and the taped-on name cards all sit at his height. Stay in the room, keep his own shoebox at the edge with the one soft toy Azlyn has signed off, and lift the nursery onto the table the moment you step out. The table knife goes back in the drawer between jobs, not left on the plate.

days.title: What the Nest Is Made Of
days.prepTonight: Tear a sheet of newspaper into strips, cut string into short lengths, pull a wad of cotton balls apart, snap a few thin twigs short, and lay all seven nest materials on the tray. Put eight dried lima beans in a bowl of water tonight, ready for Wednesday.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: A Nest for Every Small Thing

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Dry Hair and One Long Book

opening.title: Seven Things on the Tray
opening.need: the loaded tray · 1 mesh produce bag.
steps: Lay the seven nest materials you loaded onto the tray last night in a line and let her handle every one. Name them as she picks them up and let her tell you how each one feels.
Push a strand of grass through a hole in the empty mesh bag and pull it out again. Do it twice and say nothing about why.
Tell her the rule now so it has an hour to sink in: seven things on the tray, and at 9:15 she picks three.

main.title: Weaving Three Into the Mesh
materials: A few thin twigs snapped short
1 scrap of fabric torn into strips
A few feathers if you find any, otherwise more cotton balls
1 mesh produce bag, the net kind lemons come in
1 length of string to hang it by
steps: Go along the line and ask what a bird would do with each one. Take every answer, wrong ones included.
Three only. She chooses, and you move the other four to the far end of the tray where she can see what she gave up.
Write her three down on a strip of tape and stick it to the side of the bag.
She weaves the three through the net and nothing else. In one hole and out the next, ends left hanging where a beak can reach them.
Test it. She pulls one loose end the way a bird would. A single strand comes away, or half the bag comes with it.
One swap allowed. She trades one of her three for one from the reject end, weaves it in and pulls again. Tie the string on for the walk.
main.tip: Let a bad choice run to the pull test. Cotton balls empty the bag in three tugs.

outside.title: What the Birds Are Carrying
paras: Stand still somewhere with hedges and watch for birds with something in their beaks, because late March is the two weeks they are all building. Follow one until it vanishes into a hedge. Hang her mesh bag on a low branch here. Give her a paper bag for moss, thin twigs and anything a bird might want, and let her carry it home.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and can now pick up one strand of anything between finger and thumb, which is the problem with today. Give him his own job at floor level, away from the tray: a washcloth and a folded dish towel to haul out of a shoebox.

second.title: A Nest for Every Small Thing
second.intro: The moss and twigs she carried home this morning become six small nests, one for every little toy in the house.
materials: 6 paper cups or empty yogurt cups
The moss, twigs and dried grass from the morning walk
steps: Set the six cups in two rows on the tray and tip the walk bag out in the middle. Sort it with her: moss here, twigs there, grass at the end.
Tape the base of each cup to the tray. They tip over otherwise and the sorting goes with them.
Build the first one together, then hand her the tray. She does the other five while you sit at the same table doing something else.
Send her round the house for the smallest toys she can find, one per nest.
She puts each one to bed and tells you who it belongs to. Write the names on tape and stick them to the cups.
Count the nests, then the babies, and check the two numbers against each other.
Stand the tray on the counter, back from the edge and above his standing reach, where nothing can knock it. Lift it down for her at 4:15, when she comes back to it with wet hair.
second.tip: This one runs quiet if you let it. Sit down with a cup of tea and let her come and go from the tray as long as it holds her.

alternatives: Two nests instead of six, and let her keep one in her bed.
Build one big nest in the laundry basket and get in it.
Sort the walk bag by type, then by feel.
outAgain: Swimming, and she goes in first this time
The indoor play center if the pool is closed for lessons
The library on the way home for a book about birds
The park while her hair dries, if the sun holds
days.krestonPM: At 9 months he pulls to stand on the pool steps and on you, so hold him and let him do it against your chest in the shallow end. He slaps the surface with a flat hand for as long as you can stand it. Twenty minutes, then out and warm, with his cup ready because he comes out hungry.

insight.headline: Choosing three from seven is real cognitive work.
paras: Give Azlyn everything on the tray and she uses everything. Cap it at three and she has to hold the whole set in mind, picture each one working, and give four of them up, which is slow, uncomfortable work at three years old. Limits like this one are why a short list of materials produces more inventive work than a full cupboard. She commits before she knows the answer, then lives with it when the first pull empties the bag. The giving up is the hard part and it is worth sitting through. Leave the four she rejected in sight while she builds, so the choice stays real and she can see what she traded away.

days.safety: Kreston's pincer grip is new this month, so a single strand of string or a wisp of cotton balls off the carpet goes into his mouth. Work on the tray, sweep the floor before you put him down, and lift the whole tray onto the counter the moment you stop. At the pool he is held or in the stroller, never on the tiles. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Roots Against the Glass
days.prepTonight: The eight lima beans have been soaking overnight. Leave a handful more dry beside them, and dig out an envelope and a stamp for tomorrow.

opening.title: The Pot That Went Pale
opening.need: the two cress pots from last week · 2 strips of paper · a marker.
steps: Stand the pot that spent its first days shut in the cupboard beside the one off the sunny sill, and let her tell you which is which.
Tear a strip of paper level with the tallest stalk in each pot, hold the two side by side, and tape them to the window with the date on them.
Tell her the pots hide the half she cannot see. At 9:15 seven beans go in against glass, roots and all.

main.title: Roots Against the Glass
materials: 1 sheet of paper ruled into fourteen boxes, and crayons
steps: Roll two sheets of paper towels into a tube for each jar and slide them in against the glass. Scrunch more paper into the middle to hold the lining out.
Pour water down the middle, an inch, and let it wick up. Damp paper, not a swimming pool.
She posts the beans down between the glass and the paper, three or four to a jar, spaced round so none of them touch.
Mark each bean's position with tape on the outside of the glass and the date on the jar.
Ask which way the root goes and which way the shoot goes. Write her prediction on tape and stick it to the lid, wrong or right.

One jar on the windowsill, one in a dark cupboard, and tell her why the second jar exists. Rule the sheet into fourteen boxes with her, tape it to the window at her height, and let her color the first one. Both jars are hers, one box a day, at 4:00.
main.tip: Nothing shows for three or four days and she will check every hour today. The spoonful of water that tops both jars up happens at 4:00 too.

outside.title: The Branch We Come Back To
paras: Pick one branch you can reach on your usual walk and make it hers. Wrap tape round it so you can find it again. Late March has the buds fat and splitting, so let her hold one between two fingers without pulling it off. Come back every week and watch it open.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulls himself upright on anything at hip height, the windowsill included, so the jars go at the back out of reach. Give him an empty screw-top jar with a pine cone shut inside it and the lid taped on hard, checked before he gets it. He turns it over, shakes it and hunts for the noise, and nothing in it is small enough to swallow.

second.title: Down at Kreston's Height
second.intro: The morning belonged to a bean behind glass. This afternoon she crosses one room on her hands and knees, the way her brother crosses it.
materials: A cleared high shelf or cupboard top
steps: Start at the door on hands and knees and let her lead the route he takes, with your chin at her level.
Give her the rule once: anything she can lift between finger and thumb goes in the basket. Then stop pointing, and hand her the flashlight for under the sofa.
Tip the basket out and sort it into two trays, small enough for his mouth and too big for it. She decides every one, and she will measure a crayon against her own mouth to do it.
She carries the small tray up to the shelf. Write TOO SMALL FOR KRESTON on a strip of tape and let her stick it on the front.
Back down for the pull-up test. She leans her weight on every low edge, the chair legs, the toy box, the windowsill. Anything that rocks gets a tab of tape now and gets moved before he comes in.
Put him down at the door and stand back. Ask her to call which thing he goes for, then watch him prove her right or wrong.
second.tip: Take her verdicts even where you disagree, and move the one you meant to move after she is in bed. An inspector who gets overruled stops inspecting.

alternatives: One room and the sorting, then stop.
Empty one low drawer and sort that instead of the floor.
Photograph the room from his eye level and look at it together.
outAgain: The indoor play center, for an hour of running she cannot do in the house
A friend's house, if anyone is free at short notice
The garden center, to look at seed packets and name what is on the front
A walk back to your branch to show somebody else the tape
days.krestonPM: He comes in at the end of it, and the room she cleared is his to test. At 9 months he heads for the thing nobody planned for, which is the useful part. At the play center the baby area is his.

insight.headline: A daily ritual of checking teaches more than the plant does.
paras: The bean will grow whether or not Azlyn watches it. The part that changes her is the return: same jar, same time, same question, fourteen days running. A three-year-old lives in a permanent now, and a chart on the window with one box filled a day builds her a picture of time she can see. She also gets something no craft can hand her, which is a living thing that depends on her turning up. Keep the ritual small enough to survive a bad morning. Thirty seconds and a mark in a box counts as a full day of it.

days.safety: Dried beans are a choking hazard and Kreston can pick up one at a time now. Count them out and count them back, keep the jars at the back of the sill above his standing reach, and use lima beans or another white bean. Raw red kidney beans are toxic if chewed. He stays out of the room she is clearing until step six, and the small tray goes up on the shelf before he comes in.

days.title: What It Turns Into
days.prepTonight: Empty a cereal box and flatten it, put the crayons and a black marker on the table, and leave the envelope and stamp somewhere she can see them.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Pairs Game on Her Own

opening.title: Twelve Blank Cards
opening.need: 1 flattened cereal box · 1 pair of scissors (adult only) · 1 black marker.
steps: Cut twelve rectangles about the size of your palm while she holds the box steady. Keep them the same size.
Let her stack them, count them, deal them out and count them again.
Ask her to name six baby animals. Write each name on a card as she says it and leave the other six blank for the grown-ups.

main.title: The Baby and the Grown-Up
materials: Phone, for looking up what a tadpole and a caterpillar turn into
Paper and a pen for her explanations
steps: Go through her six babies and name the grown-up for each. Lamb and sheep, duckling and duck, puppy and dog, chick and hen are the four she can do. Tadpole and caterpillar are the two she cannot.
Look those two up on the phone together, and find a short clip of a tadpole growing legs.
Draw. She does the six babies, you do the six grown-ups, and neither of you comments on the other's drawing. Write the name on each card.
Spread all twelve face up on the floor and let her make the pairs. Sit on your hands.
Write down the reason she gives for each pair, word for word, wrong pairs included.
Play it again fast. Turn the twelve face down, take turns flipping two, and let her keep the ones she matches.
main.tip: She may pair the tadpole with the duckling because both live in water. A rule she built herself is the one worth coming back to in two weeks.

outside.title: The First Blossom
paras: Late March puts the first white blossom on the flowering pear and the cherry trees while everything round them is still bare. Walk until you find one, then stand under it and look up. Let her pick a fallen petal off the sidewalk instead of off the branch. Count the bare trees on the way back against the ones in flower, and tell her which way that count goes by May.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and waving at everything, including trees. Give him one of the blank cards to hold and chew while you draw. Under the blossom, hold him up so the branch is over his head. Wind through the flowers is the sort of thing he stares at with his mouth open.

second.title: The Letter to Kreston Next Spring
second.intro: She writes to her brother. The letter goes to a Kreston who does not exist yet, the one walking and talking a year from now.
materials: Phone, for a photo of him today
A pen for writing her words down as she says them
steps: Lay Kreston down and measure him with her holding one end of the tape. Write the number at the top of the first sheet with today's date.
She tells you what he is like now. His food, his tricks, the noise he makes at six in the morning. Write every word of it down without tidying it.
Then the second half: what she thinks he will be doing next spring. Give the daft answers the same weight as the sensible ones.
She draws him on the second sheet while he is in front of her.
Take a photo of the two of them together on the phone and note on the letter where it is saved.
Fold both sheets, into the envelope, and address it to Kreston at your own house. She sticks the stamp on wherever she sticks it.
She mails it herself this afternoon. It lands on the mat in a day or two, and then you write OPEN MARCH 2028 across it and put it away unopened.
second.tip: Let her carry the envelope the whole way to the mailbox and drop it in herself. It comes back through the door as mail.

alternatives: Dictate the letter only and hand-deliver it to his crib.
Draw a picture each of Kreston now and Kreston next year.
Measure everybody in the house and write the numbers on one sheet.
outAgain: The post office, with her letter, plus whatever else needs mailing
The corner store for one thing she chooses and carries home
A walk to check the blossom tree again in the afternoon light
The library, if the letter went in the box on the way past
days.krestonPM: He sits through the measuring and the drawing, then goes back to what he was doing. A line in a warm post office is decent entertainment at 9 months, because the faces are at his level and he waves at every one of them. Let him hold your keys through the line.

insight.headline: Let her hold a wrong theory for a while.
paras: Azlyn will decide that the tadpole grows up into a duck, and she will have a sound reason: they live in the same water. Correcting her on the spot hands her a fact and takes away the thinking. Children build theories about how the world works, test them against what they see, and revise when the evidence stops fitting, which is the same loop a scientist runs. Write her theory down and date it. Show her the tadpoles in the pond in three weeks and let the pond do the correcting, and the idea will stick where your answer would have slid off.

days.safety: The scissors stay with you and go back out of reach between cuts. Give Kreston a card too big to fit in his mouth and take it off him the moment it softens, because chewed card comes apart in soggy lumps. The stamp and the loose offcuts stay off the floor and above his standing reach.
